title: Education and Misinformation: Exploring Ophthalmology Content on TikTok
screen_reason: Cross-sectional content analysis of 723 popular ophthalmology TikTok videos (top 20 most-liked per each of 37 hashtags), with an explicit misinformation code fact-checked against accepted ophthalmology guidelines and published evidence. Reports the share of videos containing misinformation (5.4%, 39/723), the engagement-weighted share (4.8% of all likes, 4.7% of comments, 11.7% of bookmarks), and the severity split within the misinformation set (74.4% significant).

estimates.notes: denom_selection=curated: this is a rank-truncated 'top 20 most-liked per hashtag' set, so 5.4% is the misinformation share of POPULAR ophthalmology content, not of all ophthalmology content on TikTok. Note the definition is broader than strict falsity -- assertions 'rooted in anecdotal evidence' or in 'the absence of established scientific understanding' also qualify -- which pushes this toward the misleading end of breadth. All 39 misinformation videos were created by non-ophthalmologists and 87.2% by non-healthcare providers.

estimates.notes: Construct call for an adjudicator. Under the governing rule the denominator sets the construct: the denominator here is ENGAGEMENT (likes), which §3 assigns to SHARING (sharing_subtype content_share, i.e. share of engaged-with items that are misinformation). It is NOT exposure -- the paper does not report the share of VIEWS on misinformation videos, only likes, comments and bookmarks -- so this must not be read as an exposure estimate. Two sibling engagement metrics are reported in the same sentence and are deliberately not split into extra rows: comments 4.7% and bookmarks 11.7%. Likes is the metric with the largest and most standard denominator; the bookmark figure (11.7%) is the paper's headline disproportion claim ('received a disproportionately higher percentage of bookmarks', p = 0.001) and an adjudicator wanting the maximum engagement-weighted figure should use 11.7%.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted, with reasons: (1) SUPPLEMENTARY #EyeHealth PROBE -- 'we performed an additional TikTok search in August 2023 for the top 20 most-liked videos within the #EyeHealth hashtag and found an even higher proportion of videos containing misinformation (15%) in this term compared to the overall average percentage of videos with misinformation in this study (5.4%)'. This is a genuine second estimate (15% of 20 videos = 3/20, August 2023, a hashtag outside the 37-hashtag frame), but it is a post-hoc single-hashtag probe of n=20 that is not part of the main sample and shares the same country x platform x measure cell, so I left it out rather than risk double-counting; the full numbers are recorded here for an adjudicator who wants it. (2) Engagement-weighted shares for COMMENTS (4.7%) and BOOKMARKS (11.7%): siblings of the likes row in the same sentence, deliberately not split into separate rows (see that row's notes). (3) PEMAT-A/V understandability (mean 88.1%) and actionability (mean 50.6%) for educational videos, and the per-hashtag means in Table 1, are QUALITY scale scores reported as MEANS with no threshold share, so no QUALITY row is derivable. (4) Creator-identity distribution (ophthalmologists 16.9%, eyecare providers 35.1%, non-healthcare providers 55.0%), content-type distribution (educational 38.0%, personal experience 35.8%, entertainment 14.0%, patient experience 7.9%, promotional 4.3%), patient-experience sentiment (negative 22.8%, neutral 47.8%, positive 29.4% of 408 videos) and TikTok verification status (6.6%) are composition measures, not veracity. (5) 'all videos containing misinformation were created by non-ophthalmologists, and 87.2% were created by non-healthcare providers' -- these are shares of the misinformation set by creator type (a source composition within misinformation), not prevalences. (6) The per-hashtag counts of misinformation videos (#DryEyeSyndrome n=6, #LASIKSurgery n=4, #Conjunctivitis n=4, #LASIK n=3, ... ) are numerators without their own stated denominators (each hashtag contributed 20 videos except two, so shares could be derived, but that would be my own construction of 18 sub-rows from a pooled number, which §2 forbids). (7) The 10.1% misinformation figure for the adolescent-myopia TikTok study and the 15.1% dermatologist-creator figure are cited from other papers -- excluded by R8.

rob.design: Cross-sectional content analysis of TikTok, 16 April - 22 May 2023. Sampling frame: 37 ophthalmology-relevant hashtags (previously used in an Instagram survey, combining AAO IRIS Registry diagnostic terms with lay eye-related phrases); the top 20 most-liked videos per hashtag were analysed, yielding 723 videos and 3.806 billion views (two hashtags returned fewer than 20 eligible videos: 18 for #AgeRelatedMacularDegeneration, 5 for #Trabeculoplasty). Exclusions: veterinary ophthalmic, non-ophthalmology-related, duplicated and non-English posts. Seven coding criteria: creator identity, content type, patient-experience presence and sentiment, PEMAT-A/V understandability and actionability (educational videos only), misinformation presence (significant / minimal / none), engagement metrics, TikTok verification status. Misinformation defined as any ophthalmic assertion rooted in anecdotal evidence, falsehood or deception due to absence of established scientific understanding; suspected videos were fact-checked against accepted ophthalmology guidelines and published literature. Assessments performed by medical students and an ophthalmic clinical research coordinator under an ophthalmologist's guidance; NO inter-rater reliability statistic, rater count per video, or blinding procedure is reported -- the main risk-of-bias weakness. Sample size justified via Cochran's formula (385 sufficient; 723 analysed). Analysis in SPSS 29 with Shapiro-Wilk, Mann-Whitney U and Kruskal-Wallis H tests, alpha 0.05. IRB-exempt (public data, Common Rule Exemption 4).
